strengths: The formalization of Partially Observable Mean-Field Games with Common Noise (POMFGs-CN), and the identification of the shared-observation special case where the mean-field update remains tractable while allowing history-dependent policies, is a clean and useful contribution that plausibly fills a real gap in the MFG literature (existing HSMs and RL methods are restricted to fully observable or memoryless settings).

The unified taxonomy of DP, RL, and HSM methods (Section 3, Information Boxes 1-3) is pedagogically valuable and clearly delineates the assumptions underlying each class of methods; this framing helps position RSPG and clarifies why variance reduction is achievable.

MFAX addresses genuine limitations of existing MFG libraries (OpenSpiel, MFGLib): support for white-box dynamics, partial observability, common noise, multiple initial distributions, and the functional (non-materialized) transition operator reducing memory from O(|S|^2) to O(|S|+|S||A|+|Z|) is a well-motivated engineering contribution. Timing benchmarks (Table 2) substantiate the speed claims.

The empirical evaluation is comparatively careful: exploitability is computed exactly via backwards induction against a common, more expressive best-response class so that memoryless and history-aware methods are comparable; results are averaged over 10 seeds with 95% CI; and the hyperparameter search for RL baselines (81-243 configs vs. 3 for the HSMs) is generous to the baselines rather than to the proposed method.

Qualitative analysis (Figures 3-4) convincingly demonstrates that history-awareness yields anticipatory behavior (pre-closure movement in Beach Bar, end-of-horizon spending in Macroeconomics) that memoryless methods cannot capture, and the ablation on ordinal vs. categorical policy parameterization (Figure 11) is a nice detail.
Reproducibility is strong: the code is publicly released, pseudocode for all algorithms is provided, and environment/hyperparameter details are extensive (Appendices B and C).
weaknesses: There are no theoretical guarantees for RSPG. The paper acknowledges that restricting the policy class to shared-observation histories means the resulting policy may not be an equilibrium of the full game; because exploitability is measured against full-information best responses, zero exploitability is unreachable by construction. This means the central claim of converging to mean-field Nash equilibria is only supported heuristically ('resembles regret'), and the gap between the restricted-policy equilibrium and the true POMFG-CN equilibrium is never quantified.

The headline 'first history-aware HSM' and 'first partial-observable macroeconomics MFG with common noise' claims, while plausibly accurate, frame what is essentially a natural composition of known components (SPG + an RNN over shared observations + the observation-restriction argument) as larger conceptual advances than they are. The methodological novelty relative to Yang et al. (2025) is incremental.

The empirical scale is modest: three environments, two of which are partially observable adaptations of standard toy benchmarks (Linear Quadratic, Beach Bar) with |Z|=2 common noise realizations, and one discretized macro model. There is no evidence the approach scales to larger noise spaces, higher-dimensional aggregate states, or settings where the shared-observation assumption is violated; the paper itself concedes that RL is required when observations depend on individual states.

The evaluation depends on the assumption of known individual transition dynamics and discrete/finite policy classes for tractability of the analytic mean-field update; the continuous-action Macroeconomics case requires discretizing the policy integral, introducing approximation error that is not analyzed. Wall-clock comparisons are also implementation-dependent (both HSM and RL baselines are the authors' own JAX implementations), which somewhat weakens the 'order-of-magnitude faster' claim against external baselines.

Some presentation issues: minor grammatical/typographical errors ('the reverse it not true', 'the Bar stays closes'), inconsistent notation (Definition 2.2 vs. 5.1 restating the same equilibrium condition), and Figure 3's interpretation (spending wealth pushing interest rates 'up') would benefit from a more rigorous economic justification given the macroeconomics framing.

The exploitability curves in Figure 2 show non-trivial variance and, in some environments (e.g., Linear Quadratic), RSPG and SPG are close; the paper's claim that RSPG 'consistently' achieves the lowest exploitability is only marginally supported in the endogenous-like setting where memory matters least.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine gap: existing Hybrid Structural Methods (HSMs) for MFGs are limited to fully observable, memoryless settings, and the proposed restriction to shared aggregate observations (Section 5.1) is a clean observation that keeps the analytic mean-field update tractable while permitting history-dependent policies.
The unified taxonomy of DP, RL, and HSMs (Section 3, Information Boxes 1-3) is pedagogically useful and clarifies the information assumptions underlying each method class.

MFAX is a concrete engineering contribution: functional (non-materialised) matrix-vector products reducing memory from O(|S|^2) to O(|S| + |S||A| + |Z|), support for partial observability, common noise, and multiple initial mean-fields, with all code, hyperparameter sweeps, and compute details released (Appendix C), which aids reproducibility.

The experimental protocol is reasonably careful: wall-clock time comparisons (justified by the asymmetry between HSM expectations and RL sampling), a common best-response class for exploitability to make memoryless and history-aware methods comparable, 10 seeds with 95% CI, and large hyperparameter sweeps for baselines (81-243 configs vs 3 for RSPG), which reduces the risk of unfairly weak baselines.

The qualitative analysis (Figures 3-6) is a nice touch, demonstrating that history-aware policies learn anticipatory behaviour (Beach Bar closure, end-of-horizon spending) that memoryless policies cannot express, going beyond scalar exploitability curves.
weaknesses: No theoretical grounding whatsoever. The paper introduces a new problem formulation (POMFGs-CN) and a new equilibrium concept (Definition 5.1) but provides no existence results, no convergence analysis of RSPG, and no discussion of whether restricting the search to policies conditioning only on (s_t, o_{0:t}) preserves equilibria of the general POMFG-CN. The claim that the shared-observation restriction 'makes things computationally tractable' is asserted, not proven, and the relationship between exploitability w.r.t. the restricted class and the true Nash equilibrium distance is left informal.

The claimed novelty of 'introducing Partially Observable Mean Field Games with Common Noise' (contribution 2) is overstated. Saldi et al. (2019) and Subramanian et al. (2021) already study partially observed mean-field settings; the genuinely new part is only the common-noise-plus-shared-observation special case, which is a comparatively narrow extension and is where all the actual experiments take place. The general formulation (10)-(11) is acknowledged to be intractable and is never used.

The empirical scope is thin: two toy environments (discretised 1D state, |S|=100, finite horizon T=30) plus one macroeconomics environment that is itself finite-horizon (T=128) and discretised. For a paper claiming 'state-of-the-art performance' and 'for the first time' solving a macroeconomics MFG, there is no comparison to established macroeconomics solution methods (e.g., Krusell-Smith approximation techniques or DeepHAM, Han et al. 2022, which is cited as an HSM for exactly this setting), and no infinite-horizon evaluation despite the framework being defined for infinite horizons.

The headline 'order-of-magnitude faster convergence' and the MFAX speed claims (10x vs OpenSpiel, 1000x vs MFGLib) rest on wall-clock comparisons between a JAX/GPU implementation and libraries that are not GPU-native (OpenSpiel is C++/CPU, MFGLib is Python). This conflates library engineering with algorithmic contribution; a same-hardware, same-implementation-language comparison, or environment-step-based accounting with compute-normalised cost, is needed for the claim to be meaningful.

The exploitability metric is a custom approximation ('resembles regret') computed via backwards induction over sampled common-noise sequences with a more expressive best-response class. While the conservative upper-bound argument is reasonable, there is no validation that the approximation error is small (e.g., against a known closed-form equilibrium in the Linear Quadratic environment), so absolute exploitability values and cross-method rankings may be fragile.

The Beach Bar results depend on history capturing the timestep (the observation explicitly excludes t, Appendix B.4.2), which makes the environment almost engineered to favour recurrent policies; the ablation isolating memory value when the observation is otherwise informative (as the authors concede for the macroeconomics setting, where SPG matches RSPG) is underdeveloped.

Several presentation issues undermine polish: the abstract's URL is cut off ('MFAX is publicly available at:'), Table 3 lists |A| = ∞ and |Z| = ∞ for Macroeconomics while the text reports discretised values, notation switches between tuples with and without O/U inconsistently across Sections 2.1, 5, and the environment definitions, and typos persist ('aggregate aggregate state', 'the reverse it not true'). The impact statement is boilerplate despite macroeconomic applications that could warrant a sentence of reflection.

The 'first history-aware HSM' claim is difficult to verify and partly contested by the paper's own related work: Perrin et al. (2020) condition on common-noise histories (albeit with enumeration), and the distinction rests on the continuous-realisation and shared-observation specifics rather than a fundamental algorithmic difference.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly written problem formulation: the paper introduces Partially Observable Mean-Field Games with Common Noise (POMFGs-CN) and identifies the practically important special case of shared aggregate observations, which restores tractability of the analytic mean-field update. This special-case identification (memory restricted to the shared observation history, keeping the RNN hidden state independent of the individual state) is a genuinely insightful design choice.

RSPG is a natural and well-executed extension of Structural Policy Gradient methods (Yang et al., 2025) to history-aware policies; the manuscript appears to be correct that this is the first history-aware HSM, filling a real gap in the MFG literature.

Comprehensive unified taxonomy (Section 3, Information Boxes 1-3) of DP, RL, and HSM methods for MFGs, clearly delineating information assumptions; this is a useful contribution for readers regardless of the specific algorithm.

MFAX is a substantial practical contribution: JAX-based, distinguishes white-box vs black-box transition access, supports partial observability, common noise, and multiple initial mean-fields, and achieves large measured speedups (Table 2) over OpenSpiel and MFGLib on mean-field updates, with memory-efficient functional matrix-vector products.

Empirical evaluation is reasonably thorough for a systems paper: exploitability with a carefully argued conservative best-response class (Section 8.2.1), wall-clock comparisons over 10 seeds with 95% CIs, ablation of the ordinal action prior (Appendix C.4.1), extensive hyperparameter sweeps, and qualitative analysis (Figures 3-8) demonstrating history-dependent anticipatory behaviour in the Beach Bar and Macroeconomics environments.
Good reproducibility posture: code and hyperparameter configurations are released, environment and algorithm details (Appendices A-B) are detailed enough to reimplement.
weaknesses: No theoretical analysis. The paper provides no convergence guarantees, bias analysis, or error bounds for RSPG. Notably, gradients flow through expected rewards and individual transitions but are stopped at mean-field updates (Algorithm 1), which introduces an unspecified bias that is never quantified or empirically probed. Given the paper's positioning as the 'first history-aware HSM', at least informal justification of when this bias is acceptable would strengthen the contribution.

Limited scale and scope of experiments. All state spaces are small (100-1000 grid points, |A| <= 20 after discretisation), and the 'Macroeconomics MFG' that is claimed to be solved 'for the first time' is a finite-horizon, coarse-grid adaptation (200x5 state grid, 20 actions, T=128) of Krusell & Smith (1998) rather than the canonical infinite-horizon model; the 'for the first time' claim should be softened accordingly. Only three environments, all derived from existing MFG benchmarks.

The exploitability metric is a conservative upper bound over best responses with perfect information and provably cannot reach zero in the partially observable setting; the paper acknowledges this but never reports the absolute gap for the best achievable policy, making it hard to judge how far from equilibrium the learned policies actually are. The approximation error of the sampled-noise exploitability estimate is also not quantified.

Applicability of RSPG is quite narrow, as the authors themselves concede (Section 6.2): it requires known individual transition dynamics, tractable analytic mean-field updates, and discrete policy classes. This limits the impact relative to the abstract's framing of a general advance.

The library comparison in Table 1/2, while useful, is somewhat apples-to-oranges: OpenSpiel and MFGLib are general-purpose frameworks, and the 10x/1000x speedup headline is measured on a single environment configuration; a broader benchmark would be more convincing.

Small inconsistencies and presentation issues: Definition 2.1 states an infinite-horizon MFG while all experiments use finite horizons; the notation drifts between μ̃_t, μ_{0:t}, and M_evol; the Linear Quadratic transition (18) defines Ξ(z_{t+1}|z_t) = δ_{z_t} (no common-noise evolution) while the tuple declares common noise; Table 3 lists Macro |A| = ∞ while the action space is discretised to 20. Minor typos (e.g., 'agregate state' in B.4.2) suggest insufficient proofreading.

Hyperparameter search effort is asymmetric across methods (3 configs for SPG/RSPG vs 81-243 for baselines); the authors justify this but the possibility of sub-optimal baseline tuning in wall-clock comparisons cannot be fully excluded.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: existing methods for MFGs handle mean-field interaction, common noise, and partial observability only pairwise, and RSPG is presented as the first hybrid structural method with history-aware policies under common noise. The problem formalization (POMFG-CN) is clearly laid out, and the observation model and Assumptions 1.1 and 6.1 are explicitly stated.

The paper is unusually honest and careful about its assumptions: the authors include an explicit counter-example (Appendix A) showing that Assumption 6.1 can fail and can make the restricted policy class strictly suboptimal, and they candidly state the absence of convergence guarantees and discuss why existing theory does not transfer.

The proposed method is well-motivated technically: restricting memory to the shared public observation history keeps the mean-field a distribution over the fixed state space (Equation 13) rather than the exponentially growing history space, and the shared GRU embedding adds only a single GRU update per timestep, which is a clean and cheap design.

MFAX is a substantive artefact contribution: functional (matrix-free) evaluation of mean-field updates reducing memory from |S|^2 to O(|S| + |S||A|), support for analytic and sample-based mean-field updates, common noise, partial observability, and multiple initial distributions, with reported mean-field updates 10x-1000x faster than OpenSpiel and MFGLib on a standardized benchmark.

The experimental methodology is mostly careful: 10 seeds with 95% CIs, exploitability computed via backward induction with an exact analytic mean-field update, a larger perfect-information evaluation class used explicitly as a conservative bound, and hyperparameter budgets that favour the RL baselines (81 configurations for IPPO/RIPPO and 243 for M-OMD versus 3 for SPG/RSPG), plus ablations on policy parameterization (ordinal vs. categorical).

The qualitative results are convincing: the Beach Bar and Macroeconomics visualizations (Figures 4, 8) clearly show anticipatory behaviour (moving away from the bar before potential closure; end-of-horizon wealth spending) that memoryless baselines fail to learn, providing a concrete demonstration of what history-awareness buys.
weaknesses: No theoretical guarantees whatsoever. The central algorithmic claim (RSPG preserves HSM variance reduction while enabling history-dependent behaviour) is supported only empirically; there is no analysis of gradient variance, bias induced by Assumption 6.1, or approximation error relative to the IAOH policy class. Given the paper's own counter-example that the restriction can be strictly suboptimal, the gap between what RSPG computes and the true equilibrium is not characterized.

The core algorithmic contribution is modest: RSPG is essentially SPG with a GRU over the shared observation history. The insight is sensible but the technical machinery is an incremental extension of Yang et al. (2025), and the derivation from Equations 11-13 is straightforward once Assumption 6.1 is accepted.

The empirical scope is narrow: two toy environments with |S|=100 and one discretized macroeconomic environment. The Macroeconomics setting is admitted to be 'nearly fully observable' through prices, which weakens the evidence that the method matters precisely where partial observability is severe; no environment is included where Assumption 6.1 is genuinely strained.

The headline claim of 'order-of-magnitude faster convergence' is measured in wall-clock time, which conflates algorithmic variance reduction with implementation and structural overhead (e.g., HSMs avoid single-agent rollouts entirely, and RIPPO's sequential loss recalculation is attributed to the authors' own implementation). A step- or sample-complexity-based comparison would be more informative, even if acknowledged as not directly comparable.

The exploitability metric is computed over a perfect-information policy class for all methods, which the authors correctly note makes it a 'regret-like upper bound' rather than a distance to equilibrium; this dilutes the interpretation of the main quantitative results, and no alternative metric (e.g., restricted-class exploitability for the admissible class) is reported.

The anticipated concern that HSMs require white-box access to transition dynamics limits applicability, and the paper offers no path for settings where the analytic mean-field update is unavailable beyond future work; the practical reach of RSPG beyond the three implemented environments remains untested.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: to the authors' (plausible) knowledge, no existing method handles both common noise and partial observability in MFGs, and the formalisation of POMFGs-CN (Section 5, Equations 11-12) is a useful contribution in itself.

The writing and pedagogy are largely clear: the Information Boxes (1-3) give a well-organised taxonomy of DP, RL and HSM-based policy evaluation, and the derivation of the analytic mean-field update under the public-information restriction (Equation 13) is easy to follow.

The methodology is transparent about its limits: the authors provide an explicit counter-example showing Assumption 6.1 can fail (Appendix A), acknowledge that exploitability is measured against a larger perfect-information class rather than exact equilibrium distance, and honestly state that no convergence guarantees exist.

Reproducibility is comparatively strong: full pseudocode (Algorithms 1-3), environment specifications with all parameters (Tables 4-6), hyperparameter sweeps and compute details are provided, and the MFAX codebase is released.

MFAX is a useful systems contribution: the functional (sparse) form of the matrix-vector products reducing memory from O(|S|^2) to O(|S|+|S||A|) is a sensible engineering contribution, and the timing comparisons (Table 2) are concrete.

The empirical analysis goes beyond raw numbers: the visualisations of learned mean-fields and best-response comparisons (Figures 4-10) substantiate the claim that history-aware methods learn anticipatory behaviour (e.g., pre-closure movement in Beach Bar, end-of-horizon wealth spending in Macroeconomics).
weaknesses: The core algorithmic contribution is modest: RSPG is essentially SPG plus a GRU over the shared observation history, with mean-field updates computed per-timestep and broadcast to all states. The key design choice (restricting memory to public observations) is stated informally as an 'informational assumption' (Assumption 6.1) without any approximation-error analysis, bounds, or conditions under which the induced equilibrium is close to the IAOH-conditioned equilibrium. The paper's own counter-example shows the restriction can be strictly suboptimal, so the approximation quality is unquantified.

No theoretical guarantees of any kind are provided — not for equilibrium convergence, not for the information approximation, not for the gradient estimator. While the limitations section is candid, the central claim that RSPG 'preserves the variance-reduction benefits of HSMs' is asserted rather than demonstrated (no variance measurements are reported).

The experimental scope is narrow and, critically, the environments do not stress-test the method: Linear Quadratic and Beach Bar are small (|S|=100, |Z|=2) toy problems, and the authors themselves concede the Macroeconomics environment is 'nearly fully observable'. There is no experiment where partial observability is severe and the public-history assumption is genuinely load-bearing, so the claim of learning 'history-aware behaviour' in challenging partially observable settings rests on weak evidence.

The headline 'order-of-magnitude faster convergence' is a wall-clock comparison against model-free baselines that the authors design to be slower by construction (single-agent rollouts between mean-field rollouts, sequential loss recalculation for RIPPO). Since HSMs exploit white-box dynamics that RL baselines deliberately do not use, the speed-up is unsurprising; the fair and informative comparison (SPG with MLP vs RSPG) shows comparable exploitability in the most realistic environment, weakening the marginal value of the recurrence.

The 'first history-aware HSM' claim is contestable given DeepHAM (Han et al., 2021), which the paper itself classifies as an HSM and which operates on aggregate shocks with history-dependent neural policies; the distinction relies on the authors' specific definition and deserves more careful justification.

Several claims are supported only by assertion: the behavioural realism of the learned Macroeconomics equilibrium (spending near end-of-episode) is described as 'more realistic' without reference to any economic benchmark or validation; the exploitability upper-bound framing (Π_PI) means RSPG's 'lowest or second-lowest exploitability' does not directly measure equilibrium quality.

Presentation issues: the abstract ends with 'can be found at' followed by no URL; notation is heavy and inconsistently styled (bold vs. non-bold for distributions); the taxonomy sections partly restate SPG material at length; some citations are to works dated 2026 that cannot be verified.
The MFAX contribution, while useful, is primarily engineering; the scientific novelty of the paper is carried almost entirely by RSPG, which is a small delta over prior work.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formalized problem: the paper is, to the authors' credible knowledge, the first to treat MFGs with both common noise and partial observability, and it carefully defines the POMFG-CN setting, the history-space intractability, and the resulting mean-field update equations (Equations 11-13).

The unified taxonomy of DP / RL / Hybrid Structural Methods (Section 4, Information Boxes 1-3) is a genuine pedagogical contribution that the MFG literature lacks, and it precisely situates RSPG's variance-reduction mechanism.

Intellectual honesty: the authors provide a counter-example (Appendix A) showing Assumption 6.1 does not hold universally, explicitly restrict the policy class, and candidly acknowledge the absence of convergence guarantees and why existing theory does not transfer.

Solid empirical methodology: exploitability computed via backward induction with exact analytic mean-field updates, 10 seeds with 95% CIs, wall-clock comparisons with justification, extensive hyperparameter sweeps that actually favor the baselines (81 configurations for IPPO/RIPPO, 243 for M-OMD vs. 3 for SPG/RSPG), and qualitative visualizations (Figures 4-10) that demonstrate anticipatory history-dependent behaviour.

MFAX is a substantive artifact: functional-form matrix-vector products reduce memory from |S|^2 to O(|S|+|S||A|), benchmarked speedups over OpenSpiel and MFGLib (Table 2), and support for common noise, partial observability, and multiple initial mean-fields that existing libraries lack (Table 1).
Useful ablations, e.g., the ordinal vs. categorical action parameterization (Appendix D.4.1, Figure 11) explains why Q-function-based M-OMD underperforms and is a finding of independent interest.
weaknesses: No theoretical results: there are no convergence, variance-reduction, or approximation-error guarantees for RSPG. All central claims are empirical, and the empirical evidence rests on only three environments (two small toy tasks with |S|=100 and one discretized macroeconomics model), limiting the generality of the order-of-magnitude convergence claim.

Assumption 6.1 is restrictive and the authors' own counter-example shows it can fail in payoff-relevant ways; restricting the equilibrium search to policies conditioning on (st, o0:t) may therefore exclude genuine Nash equilibria, and the paper does not quantify how binding this restriction is in the tested environments.

The exploitability metric is computed over the perfect-information class Π_PI, making it a 'conservative regret-like upper bound' rather than true distance to equilibrium; this weakens the interpretation of Figure 2, since methods could look competitive under a metric that does not exactly measure equilibrium proximity in the admissible class.

Comparisons rely on wall-clock time and the authors' own implementations of all baselines; the claimed advantage over RL methods partially reflects architectural choices (e.g., no single-agent rollouts between mean-field rollouts), and M-OMD's poor performance is attributed to an implementation-level parameterization issue rather than a fundamental limitation.

The distinction between RSPG and SPG is modest in aggregate terms: exploitability curves are often close (e.g., Macroeconomics), and the history-awareness benefit is demonstrated mostly through qualitative visualizations rather than a quantitative measure of the value of memory.

Partial observability in the tested environments is relatively mild (agents observe mean state, prices, or bar location but not timestep/noise), so the method's behavior under genuinely informative private observations or individual-state-dependent observation kernels (which the formalism in Section 5 allows but experiments do not exercise) remains untested.

Scalability claims for MFAX and RSPG are not stress-tested beyond |S|=1000 with a 5-point income grid; the exponentially growing history space is avoided by assumption, and behavior when the public observation channel is weakly informative is not explored.
